Article Title: Apple may launch its first touch-screen MacBook on October 27: Report
Article Text:
Apple may launch its first touch-screen MacBook on October 27

What to expect from Apple’s rumoured October 27 event

Apple announces ‘Welcome home’ event for October 13

Apple is planning to introduce its first MacBook with touch screen on October 27, reports Bloomberg citing people with knowledge of the matter. The end-of-month announcements will also include versions of the 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac with M6 chips, said the source cited by the publication. As per the report, the company may also bring a new iPad mini at the event. The reported October 27 event will follow the October 13 event where the company will unveil its revamped smart home strategy. Like its smart home event on October 13, the next launch will include an online video presentation and in-person component for the press, the report says.As stated in the Bloomberg report, the company will debut both MacBooks and iPad later this month. The new lineup, it says, “will be geared toward creative professionals who work in video production, photo editing and music production”.Further, the unveilings are said to be part of a record-setting slate of fresh products under new CEO John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook last month. Tetanus is reportedly aiming to steer the tech giant into new markets and bolster revenue from related services.Meanwhile, the company has announced a ‘Welcome home’ event for October 13.Apple’s SVP of Worldwide Marketing, Greg Joswiak posted a teaser video of the launch on X. The company is expected to unveil its “long-awaited smart home hub with a screen, the new HomePod mini and an updated Apple TV.The most notable launch is expected to be a new smart home hub with a built-in display, which could compete with devices such as Google Nest Hub and Amazon Echo Show. The device is rumoured to feature an S11 chip, which could support faster performance and Siri AI features. The screen could be used to show information such as weather updates, calendar events and music controls.A FaceTime camera is also among the expected features, potentially allowing the device to double as a video-calling hub. Apple is also reportedly developing a specialised operating system for the device focused on smart home controls.
Article Summary: Apple is planning to introduce its first MacBook with touch screen on October 27, reports Bloomberg citing people with knowledge of the matter. The end-of- month announcements will also include versions of the 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac with M6 chips, said the source cited by the publication. The reported October 27 event will follow the October 13 event where the company will unveil its revamped smart home strategy.

Article Title: Meet Caden Terence Pohlkamp, a teenager from Texas, who built an aquatic robot to save fish and other aquatic life in ponds across the State
Article Text:
What Caden’s aquatic robot found in Texas ponds

From an underwater rover to local environmental research

A Texas teenager has built an aquatic robot to help save fish. Caden Terence Pohlkamp, currently a middle school student, used robotics to study retention ponds and how well they support aquatic life. In coastal Texas communities, retention ponds are important systems for managing stormwater and reducing flood risks. But these man-made reservoirs can also become habitats for fish and other aquatic creatures. Balancing their role in flood management with their ability to support wildlife is not always straightforward. Caden, who is a 7th-grader from Friendswood, decided to investigate the issue himself.According to the Society for Science, Caden wanted to find out if there was an “optimal way to design them to provide suitable habitats for the local marine life.” To do that, he engineered an aquatic remote-operated vehicle that could travel underwater and collect samples without disturbing the ponds.The project combined his interest in marine biology and robotics. Instead of manually entering the ponds or relying only on surface observations, Caden’s submersible data-gatherer let him collect water samples from the bottom of 12 ponds across his town.This approach gave him comparable data across different retention ponds and helped him examine the conditions aquatic animals need to survive.After collecting samples, Caden analysed the water for factors that can affect aquatic life. His research focused on pH levels, turbidity (how cloudy the water is), and dissolved oxygen.The results showed that some design features made retention ponds more suitable for aquatic life. The healthier ponds had between 15% and 30% non-grass vegetation along their edges and also contained fountains. These ponds recorded higher levels of dissolved oxygen, an important factor for fish and other aquatic organisms.Caden learned that plants and trees along the edges could provide habitat for fish and help prevent algae blooms. Excessive algae can remove oxygen from the water, creating more difficult conditions for aquatic life.Caden did not stop after collecting and analysing the samples. He presented his findings to local officials, giving them information that could help identify retention ponds where changes might improve conditions for aquatic life.His project shows how a relatively small robotics experiment can help study an environmental issue in a local community. The aquatic robot allowed Caden to gather information from places that would have been difficult to study consistently without an underwater vehicle.The project also reflects the connection between infrastructure and wildlife in growing coastal communities. Retention ponds are built primarily for stormwater management, but their design can influence whether they also become useful habitats for fish and other organisms.For Caden, the experiment has also connected two interests that could shape his future. By combining robotics with marine biology, the 7th-grader has already begun exploring how technology can help us understand and protect aquatic ecosystems. His underwater rover may have started as a school project, but the data it collected gave him a practical way to study the ponds in his own community.
Article Summary: Caden Terence Pohlkamp, currently a middle school student, used robotics to study retention ponds and how well they support aquatic life. In coastal Texas communities, retention ponds are important systems for managing stormwater and reducing flood risks. Balancing their role in flood management with their ability to support wildlife is not always straightforward.

Article Title: Anthropic is updating its Claude usage policy for the first time after almost a year, may start 'banning' users who ...
Article Text:
What new policy says on abusive behavior towards Claude

Consolidated rules under new sections, clarifying weapons prohibition and more

Anthropic makes ‘not without humans’ guideline clear for Claude

AI giant Anthropic has implemented updates to its acceptable usage policy for the first time in over a year. The changes announced aim to establish strict guardrails against emerging threats such as weaponization, illicit surveillance, and election manipulation, while introducing a unique provision that shields its AI model Claude, from user cruelty.The most unconventional addition explicitly prohibits "sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior" directed at the AI model itself. Building on an initiative announced last August that permitted Claude to sever interactions with persistently abusive individuals as part of ongoing "model welfare" research. The company confirmed that conversation termination remains its primary remedy. While Anthropic has not clarified whether bad actors might face permanent account bans.Here's what Anthropic policy on banning abusive behaviour towards Claude says, "We’ve added a prohibition on sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models. The policy update is meant to apply only in extreme cases, where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose. It does not apply to common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research.It adds, "This addition aligns with a step we've already taken, allowing Claude models to end rare conversations with persistently abusive users on Claude.ai and Claude Code. Such abuse is the main focus of this update; Claude’s ability to end these interactions will remain the primary enforcement mechanism."At the same time, the revision sharply targets high-stakes public concerns surrounding deceptive influence operations. Anthropic consolidated several disparate rules into a unified prohibition against covert commercial or political campaigns, explicitly outlawing the use of fake accounts and synthetic amplification to hide who is generating content. The framework also clamps down on election interference, outlawing candidate impersonation, voting misinformation, and coordinated attempts to suppress turnout.Heightened safeguards around military hardware and digital tracking form another pillar of the update. Although Anthropic has long prohibited direct weapons development, company notes in its updated policy that bad actors have repeatedly attempted to harness Claude for targeting guidance and control systems. Consequently, the expanded rules now explicitly bar the creation of operational components for weaponry, including the arming of aerial drones and autonomous platforms.The move reportedly follows findings from the company’s internal threat intelligence reports showing that malicious actors were increasingly attempting to leverage Claude to identify and hunt political dissidents. Under the clarified surveillance ban, any nonconsensual tracking -- whether in real time or through historical data mining -- is strictly forbidden. The system is likewise barred from being used to build surveillance infrastructure or make determinations regarding criminal investigations, arrests, and charging decisions, though Anthropic noted that specific government contracts may permit customized exceptions if appropriate safeguards are established.Anticipating the rapid convergence of artificial intelligence and physical robotics, the policy also introduces mandatory human oversight whenever Claude is integrated with real-world machinery. If the AI is connected to autonomous physical hardware capable of causing bodily injury, a qualified operator must maintain constant visibility and possess the immediate authority to halt operations, setting a cautious baseline as the industry pushes deeper into embodied AI and industrial automation.
Article Summary: Anthropic announces updates to its acceptable usage policy for the first time in over a year. Changes aim to establish strict guardrails against emerging threats such as weaponization, illicit surveillance, and election manipulation. The most unconventional addition explicitly prohibits "sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior" directed at the AI model itself.

Article Title: 38 BEST blade battery e-buses arrive; Rollout of 49 next-gen vehicles in a week
Article Text:
The buses will have lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries integrated directly into the bus chassis





Mumbai: A fleet of nine new blade battery buses arrived at the Magathane depot on Saturday, with a total of 49 new tech e-buses expected to arrive within a week, according to a senior official.The new induction features next-generation electric buses manufactured by Olectra Greentech Limited, powered by advanced Blade Battery technology designed for lower risk, longer operating range and fast-charging capabilities.Said a senior official: “Our fleet of buses is over 2,800 at present and with the new buses joining the fleet, it could cross 2,900. The new buses will be deployed on longer routes connecting south Mumbai to suburbs and some from city to Navi Mumbai. These buses are safe and can run longer distances than the existing e-buses in our fleet.”The buses will have lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries integrated directly into the bus chassis. Designed for enhanced safety, longer range and lower operating costs, these compact and lightweight batteries offer at least 30% more energy storage than those currently used in electric AC buses, while significantly improving overall vehicle stability and space efficiency.While existing electric buses cover around 250 km on a single charge, the new Blade Battery fleet boasts a range of 325 km to 500 km. Even on congested city roads, they guarantee a minimum range of 325 km, allowing up to two days of continuous operation without returning to the depot for recharging.Charging efficiency has also received a massive upgrade. Sources indicate that standard high-power depot DC fast chargers can power the battery from 30% to 80% in just 30 to 45 minutes. A complete 100% top-up typically takes one to two hours to protect long-term cell health.Blade Battery technology is globally recognised for superior thermal safety, featuring reduced heat generation and non-oxygen release during high stress. “Blade battery is designed to withstand extreme climatic conditions and is much safer even when severely damaged during accidents,” stated an official from Olectra Greentech. With battery life exceeding 5,000 charge cycles, replacement and maintenance costs will be drastically reduced over the vehicle’s operational lifecycle.
Article Summary: A fleet of nine new blade battery buses arrived at the Magathane depot on Saturday. A total of 49 new tech e-buses are expected to arrive within a week. The buses will have lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries integrated directly into the bus chassis.

Article Title: Four bins, QR codes: How ward 80 got waste segregation right
Article Text:
While source segregation struggles across Madurai, 80th ward in Jaihindpuram has achieved nearly 90% segregation and a 50% improvement in waste collection.

Madurai

:





While Madurai’s waste segregation drive struggled with irregular collection and inadequate vehicles, ward 80 in Jaihindpuram increased daily segregation from 52% on September 1 up to 89% by month-end through dedicated vehicles, digital monitoring and incentives.Launched by deputy mayor T Nagarajan, the initiative covers around 3,500 households in zone 5. Residents segregate wet, dry, sanitary and special-care waste into green, blue, red and black bins, respectively, provided through CSR funding.Five dedicated vehicles cover the ward’s five sub-zones daily. The corporation partnered with Sethu Institute of Technology’s technical division to install QR codes at every household, which sanitation workers scan during collection. An app awards households five points for segregating all four categories, two for separating two categories and none for mixed waste. The system also helps officials verify daily collections and monitor workers’ performance.While the recent sanitation workers’ strike left garbage accumulating in FF Nagar and Aruldosspuram, Jaihindpuram resumed collection and cleaning quickly, aided by digital monitoring. With monthly incentives encouraging participation, corporation officials plan to replicate the model citywide as ward 80 works towards 100% segregation.
Article Summary: ward 80 in Jaihindpuram increased daily segregation from 52% on September 1 up to 89% by month-end. The initiative covers around 3,500 households in zone 5. Residents segregate wet, dry, sanitary and special-care waste into green, blue, red and black bins.

Article Title: In 1967, an Australian man built a house from thousands of discarded glass bottles; nearly 60 years later, the unusual Lightning Ridge building survives as a mining museum and tourist attraction
Article Text:
The Bottle House was built in 1967 and remains one of the distinctive landmarks in Lightning Ridge.

How discarded bottles became building material

The building's walls are its most distinctive feature. Rows of glass bottles form the structure, giving it an appearance unlike a conventional house made with bricks, timber or concrete.

From a miner's camp to a museum

Today, the building houses a small museum featuring objects linked to opal mining and minerals.

Where visitors can see the Bottle House

The attraction offers a look at both the region's mining heritage and an unusual approach to construction.

Thousands of discarded glass bottles became the building material for an unusual house in the Australian outback in 1967. Nearly six decades later, the structure still stands in Lightning Ridge, New South Wales, where it serves as a tourist attraction and a museum displaying opal-mining artefacts, vintage bottles and other historical objects. Known as the Bottle House, the building was constructed by Tex Moeckel. Its walls are made from glass bottles fixed together, while its sharply pitched, almost A-frame roof is covered with corrugated iron. Inside, the building has several small rooms and a loft.According to the official website of the New South Wales government, the Bottle House was built in 1967 and remains one of the town's distinctive landmarks. It also lists it as the Bottle House and Mining Museum, describing it as an example of unusual architecture and resourcefulness in a former mining camp.The Bottle House was created using bottles collected from Hebel, a small town across the Queensland border. According to the New South Wales Government's official tourism information, the bottles were initially joined using cement. Moeckel later discovered that local clay was more suitable because it made it easier to replace a bottle if it broke. The building's walls are its most distinctive feature. Rows of glass bottles form the structure, giving it an appearance unlike a conventional house made with bricks, timber or concrete.Light passing through the glass creates another visual feature, highlighted in the official tourism website's photo gallery. The available historical records do not specify the exact number of bottles used in the construction. However, the building's walls are made almost entirely from bottles, making discarded glass the defining element of its design.The Bottle House was originally associated with a miner's camp, reflecting Lightning Ridge's history as an opal-mining settlement. The town, in northern New South Wales, is widely known for its black opals and has a long history of mining and small-scale settlement. As reported by The Lightning Ridge Historical Society, Dave Martin operated the Bottle House for a period during the 1970s. An advertisement for the attraction appeared in the local Lightning Flash newspaper in September 1969, indicating that it was being promoted to visitors soon after it was built.Today, the building houses a small museum featuring objects linked to opal mining and minerals. Visitors can also see a collection of vintage bottles, artworks and other old items. The collection extends beyond the bottles incorporated into the walls, giving the attraction a broader connection to local history.The Bottle House and Mining Museum is located on Opal Street in Lightning Ridge, New South Wales, postcode 2834. According to the New South Wales Government's website, the listed admission price ranges from 2 to 10 Australian dollars (AUD). Visitors who need accessibility information are advised to contact the venue before visiting. The attraction offers a look at both the region's mining heritage and an unusual approach to construction. Its glass-bottle walls remain the main draw, while the mining artefacts and vintage objects provide additional context about the area.Built in 1967 by Tex Moeckel, the Bottle House has survived as a reminder of a time when discarded materials were used to create a distinctive local building. It now serves a different purpose from its early days as part of a miner's camp: preserving and displaying pieces of Lightning Ridge's history for visitors.
Article Summary: The Bottle House was built in Lightning Ridge, New South Wales, in 1967. Its walls are made from glass bottles fixed together, while its sharply pitched, almost A-frame roof is covered with corrugated iron. Today, the building houses a small museum featuring objects linked to opal mining and minerals.

Article Title: Baltimore turned waste glass into road surfaces on at least 17 streets; the crushed glass made the pavement sparkle under sunlight and streetlights
Article Text:
PC: AI Generated

How did Baltimore’s recycled glass roads create a sparkling effect

PC: AI Generated

How is crushed glass turned into a paving material

Crushed glass can affect the strength and performance of asphalt

What makes recycled glass suitable for asphalt paving

At least 17 streets in Baltimore were paved with recycled glass, creating road surfaces that could sparkle when sunlight or streetlights hit them. Baltimore's approach is part of a broader practice of using crushed waste glass in asphalt mixes. Properly processed glass can replace some of the conventional aggregate used in road construction.Wearing surfaces containing 10 to 15% crushed glass have performed well. According to the Federal Highway Administration, recycled glass has also been used in road projects elsewhere in the United States. New York City used about 225,000 metric tonnes of glass in resurfacing applications between 1990 and 1995.However, earlier projects found problems when glass was used in high percentages or as large pieces. The guidance recommends using properly processed glass in suitable proportions for asphalt paving.Waste glass was tested for use in hot mix asphalt during field demonstrations in the United States in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Test paving strips were placed at about 33 locations across the United States and Canada. Baltimore later used glass in at least 17 streets, producing a sparkle effect from reflected sunlight or street lamp light.Early projects often used more than 25% glass and coarse particles. The guidance says high glass percentages and large particles probably contributed to stripping and raveling problems reported during those demonstrations. Glass does not absorb asphalt cement binder and bonds poorly to it. Moisture damage can become a concern when high percentages and large gradations are used in surface mixes.According to the FHWA guidance, turning waste glass into a suitable paving material requires several processing steps before it can be mixed into the asphalt. Waste glass is first cleaned to remove materials such as metal, plastic, and paper. It is then crushed and screened to produce smaller, more suitable pieces while removing flat, elongated, and sharp-edged particles.For surface pavements, the guidance recommends using glass smaller than 4.75 mm, or the No. 4 sieve, as a fine aggregate mixed with conventional materials. Asphalt wearing surfaces containing 10 to 15% crushed glass have shown satisfactory performance. Higher proportions, potentially up to 25%, may be suitable for base or binder courses, where the glass is not exposed directly at the road surface.Well-crushed glass can also affect the performance of asphalt mixes because of its angular shape and high friction angle. The guidance says these properties can contribute to good lateral stability, with tests reporting stability comparable to, and in many cases better than, conventional mixes. Waste glass also has a specific gravity about 10 to 15% below that of conventional aggregates, which can increase the yield of an asphalt mix.Its low thermal conductivity may also help mixes containing glass retain heat for longer. Skid resistance tests on pavements containing waste glass have produced results within recommended limits. However, larger glass particles measuring more than 19 mm can become slippery when wet and should not be used in surface mixes. The guidance also notes that using more than 15% glass can increase pavement reflectivity and glare, particularly when the surface is wet.Asphalt mixes containing crushed glass can be designed using standard laboratory procedures. The guidance recommends testing the mix for stripping potential and says conventional pavement structural design methods are appropriate.Most highway departments allow 5 to 10% glass. The guidance says performance is generally best when crushed glass is used as a sand or fine aggregate substitute.The same methods and equipment can be used to store, mix, place, and compact asphalt containing waste glass. Field testing should follow the procedures used for conventional hot mix asphalt. The guidance identifies a need for uniform specifications covering sizing, debris levels, and mix limitations. It says a lack of adequate and consistent glass supply remains a major constraint on wider use.
Article Summary: At least 17 streets in Baltimore were paved with recycled glass. Glass can replace some of the conventional aggregate used in road construction. New York City used about 225,000 metric tonnes of glass in resurfacing applications between 1990 and 1995. Earlier projects found problems when glass was used in high percentages or as large pieces.

Article Title: A 3D-printed bridge inspired by Leonardo da Vinci uses waste stone and marble powder; 13 printed blocks form a self-supporting structure
Article Text:
Representative Image of a modern bridge inspired by Leonardo da Vinci and built with 3D printing technology ( AI Generrated Image)

Da Vinci's Bridge: how 3D printing brings Leonardo's design into the modern era

Inside the material: mortar made with 30% waste stone and marble powders

Stereotomy and self-support: how 13 printed blocks form the bridge

Da Vinci's Bridge: how 3D printing brings Leonardo's design into the modern era

Inside the material: mortar made with 30% waste stone and marble powders

Stereotomy and self-support: how 13 printed blocks form the bridge

A bridge inspired by a design sketched by Leonardo da Vinci more than 500 years ago has been brought to life as a modern prototype using 3D printing and waste from stone processing. WASP and the Polytechnic University of Bari said, the project team describes Da Vinci's Bridge as the first 3D-printed bridge to use waste materials from stone processing , combining additive manufacturing with Leonardo's original vision for a self-supporting structure. The project was conceived by Professor Giuseppe Fallacara of the Polytechnic University of Bari and draws on Leonardo's design for a bridge that would have connected the Pera district, present-day Galata in Beyoğlu, with Constantinople, today's Istanbul, across the Golden Horn. The prototype is a pedestrian bridge with a span of approximately 6 metres and adapts Leonardo's concept for the needs of the experiment.The project's distinctive feature is not simply that the bridge was 3D-printed, but that its construction material incorporates waste from stone and marble processing. B&Y, an Italian start-up led by Vincenzo Gurrado, developed a low-environmental-impact mortar made from 30% waste stone and marble powders combined with a lime-based binder. The project brought together the ArCoD department of the Polytechnic University of Bari with WASP, which supplied the 3D-printing technology, and B&Y, which developed the material.The project demonstrates how waste generated during stone processing can be incorporated into a material for 3D-printed construction rather than being treated solely as a disposal problem.Leonardo's original bridge was never built, but its design was notable for its self-supporting form. The modern project does not reproduce the proposed structure at its original scale. Instead, Fallacara's team adapted the concept into a roughly 6-metre pedestrian prototype, allowing the researchers to test the combination of 3D printing, stone-processing waste and the geometric principles behind Leonardo's design.Turning the material into a physical bridge required large-format 3D printing. WASP provided its machines and technical expertise for producing the blocks that form the structure. The bridge was divided into 13 blocks with variable layers, each printed using the WASP 3MT LDM Concrete, a large-format printer designed for cementitious materials. The printed blocks were then assembled by the University of Bari using a system of temporary centering, which supported the pieces during construction.Once the blocks were assembled, the temporary supports could be removed. The completed structure is able to support itself through the principle of stereotomy, which was also central to Leonardo's original bridge concept. In this approach, the geometry and arrangement of individual structural pieces allow them to work together as a self-supporting whole. The project therefore combines a historical construction principle with a contemporary manufacturing process rather than simply reproducing Leonardo's drawing in a different material.The use of stereotomy is key to the bridge's structure. Leonardo's original design relied on the arrangement of individual elements to create a self-supporting form, and the modern prototype applies the same underlying principle to its 13 3D-printed blocks. The temporary centring system was used during assembly, but the finished bridge does not depend on those temporary supports to remain standing. When the project was reported in January 2025, the team said its next steps included evaluating the material's mechanical properties and refining the printing process.A bridge inspired by a design sketched by Leonardo da Vinci more than 500 years ago has been brought to life as a modern prototype using 3D printing and waste from stone processing. In this approach, the geometry and arrangement of individual structural pieces allow them to work together as a self-supporting whole. The project therefore combines a historical construction principle with a contemporary manufacturing process rather than simply reproducing Leonardo's drawing in a different material.The use of stereotomy is key to the bridge's structure. Leonardo's original design relied on the arrangement of individual elements to create a self-supporting form, and the modern prototype applies the same underlying principle to its 13 3D-printed blocks. The temporary centring system was used during assembly, but the finished bridge does not depend on those temporary supports to remain standing. When the project was reported in January 2025, the team said its next steps included evaluating the material's mechanical properties and refining the printing process.
Article Summary: A bridge inspired by a design sketched by Leonardo da Vinci more than 500 years ago has been brought to life as a modern prototype using 3D printing and waste from stone processing. The project was conceived by Professor Giuseppe Fallacara of the Polytechnic University of Bari and draws on Leonardo's design for a bridge that would have connected the Pera district, present-day Galata in Beyoğlu, with Constantinople. The prototype is a pedestrian bridge with a span of approximately 6 metres and adapts Leonardo's concept for the needs of the experiment.

Article Title: In 2015, volunteers removing litter from an Irish beach spotted an unknown prehistoric shell midden, adding a newly recorded archaeological site to Sligo’s coastline
Article Text:
Representative AI image of workers collecting debris during a coastal cleanup. Image Credits: Google Gemini.

A shell layer hidden beneath the dunes

What the midden revealed

A dedicated volunteer discovered a prehistoric midden during a beach cleanup in Sligo back in May 2015. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

When erosion uncovers the past

A routine beach clean is usually measured in bags of plastic, bottles and other debris removed from the sand. But in May 2015, a group of volunteers on Ireland’s County Sligo coast came across something far older. While clearing litter at Rosses Point, Martina Butler noticed a thin, unusual layer of oyster shells exposed along the edge of a dune.According to the MASC Project, the discovery initially appeared out of place among the modern rubbish. The shells were later identified as a possible prehistoric midden, a refuse deposit left by people who gathered and ate shellfish. The find mattered not only for its archaeological value, but also because a member of the public spotted it without formal archaeological training.Butler was participating in a beach clean-up organised by the North West Sea Kayaking Association under the 'Clean Coasts' initiative. It was on 15 May 2015 that Butler observed this distinctive shell layer along with burnt material in the darker sediment layer underneath. She had previously seen middens elsewhere on the Sligo coast, so she suspected this feature could also be archaeological.She took photographs of the site and then notified the Monitoring the Archaeology of Sligo’s Coastline, or MASC, project the next day. This mattered because shell deposits on beaches are not always archaeological in origin. Waves have been known to gather the shells at the high-tide mark, while fires on the beach create artificial charcoal and stones.A member of MASC visited the site, recorded its GPS coordinates and photographed the visible remains. The dense collection of oyster and periwinkle shells, along with charcoal in the deposit, strengthened the case that people had used the site. The Archaeological Survey of Ireland also checked it out. Eleven days after the discovery by Butler, it was registered as an archaeological monument under RMP No. SL008-203.The newly uncovered midden is small. Its deposit is about 6.5 metres long and 1.2 metres in width, while its depth varies from just a few millimetres to about 10 centimetres. It is composed mainly of oysters, along with some periwinkles, stones and charcoal. For archaeologists, such waste can provide information about how the coast was used in the past. Middens are food waste deposits that can reveal what people collected and ate. Shell types, charcoal, and other waste can be used by scientists to study the ways the coast was utilised and whether there was repeated or brief settlement.Research on shell middens has shown how these deposits can preserve evidence of long-term relationships between coastal communities and marine resources. Work published in the Journal of Archaeological Science has demonstrated the value of analysing shell assemblages and their surrounding deposits to reconstruct past human use of coastal environments. The Sligo find could not be dated precisely. According to the researchers at MASC, middens in Ireland can range from the Mesolithic Era, circa 8,000-4,500 BC, all the way up until later periods. However, the thin layer of material at the Rosses Point site may indicate a brief, possibly seasonal occupation.However, the discovery also came with a risk. The erosion of the dunes that uncovered the site was also putting it at risk. The deposit lay beneath dune sand on a harder stone surface. Tides and storms in 2014 and 2015 eroded the dune and exposed the archaeology. For example, the MASC Project was created because erosion and storms kept revealing archaeological sites along the Sligo coast. In 2015, it was reported that there were 148 sites at risk of archaeological monuments located only 10 meters away from the coast, where five new monuments not previously identified were discovered through citizen science.The findings of later archaeology in Sligo have further confirmed the fragility of such coastal deposits. Shell middens have been recorded as being exposed in eroding cliffs and dunes, with some sites containing shell, faunal bone, charcoal, and fire-cracked rocks. The researchers have warned that any future storms could remove archaeological evidence before it is recorded. Butler’s discovery was not only an unusual beach-cleaning find; it also showed how people using the coastline can act as extra eyes for archaeologists.
Article Summary: A volunteer discovered a prehistoric midden during a beach cleanup in Sligo back in May 2015. Middens are food waste deposits that can reveal what people collected and ate. Shell middens in Ireland can range from the Mesolithic Era, circa 8,000-4,500 BC, all the way up until later periods.

Article Title: Beneath one Sussex wind turbine, 75,000 recycled cubes replace rock armour in the ocean; could create more than twice the potential marine habitat
Article Text:
Representative AI image

Why the wind turbine needs protection

What are the 75,000 cubes?

How could they help marine life?

Why the habitat claim is still being tested

A test for future offshore wind farms

About 75,000 recycled concrete cubes have been installed around the foundation of a wind turbine at the Rampion Offshore Wind Farm, about 13 kilometres off the Sussex coast in the English Channel. The unusual installation is designed to do two jobs at once: protect the turbine foundation from seabed erosion, known as scour, and create additional spaces that marine organisms can potentially use as shelter or attachment points. The cubes replace conventional rock-based scour protection at one turbine and form part of a project called Reef Enhancement for Scour Protection, or RESP. The developers say the design could provide more than twice the potential habitat volume of traditional rock protection, although the ecological benefits are still being monitored.Offshore wind turbines need protection from scour, which occurs when waves and currents remove seabed sediment around their foundations. If left uncontrolled, this erosion can expose or undermine parts of a turbine foundation. Rock armour is commonly used to stabilise the seabed around offshore structures, creating a protective layer that reduces the movement of sediment.At Rampion, the RESP project is testing whether that necessary engineering protection can also be designed to provide greater ecological complexity.The trial is located at turbine J04, where a scour pit of roughly 2 to 3 metres had developed. Instead of relying solely on conventional rock, engineers installed a specially designed array of concrete Reef cubes around the foundation.The installation contains about 75,100 Reef cubes weighing approximately 1,735 tonnes in total. The cubes come in different sizes and designs, including larger units with internal chambers and passageways. Their rough surfaces also contain features such as cracks, pits and crevices intended to create additional spaces for marine organisms.The system was developed by UK marine-design company ARC marine in collaboration with RWE. The cubes were manufactured in the UK using a material that ARC marine describes as 98% recycled, while the design was developed to withstand the forces experienced around an offshore turbine. The installation covers roughly 820 square metres of seabed.The Reef cubes are intended to create a more complex three-dimensional habitat than a conventional layer of rock. Their internal chambers can provide sheltered spaces, while their textured surfaces offer potential attachment points for organisms living on or around the seabed.Species identified as potential users of the structures include European seabass, black seabream, brown crab, common starfish, European flat oysters and Ross worms. The structures could also provide refuge for smaller organisms and juvenile fish. However, these are potential ecological benefits rather than evidence that the installation has already produced a measured increase in marine populations.The claim that the cubes can more than double marine habitat refers to the potential habitat volume created by the design, rather than a finding that the amount of marine life has already doubled. RWE and ARC marine have compared the geometry of the Reef cube system with conventional rock scour protection and say it can provide more than twice the potential habitat volume.The distinction matters because the installation is also an ecological experiment. RWE says surveys are planned in 2026, 2028 and 2030 to examine how organisms colonise the structure and compare the results with other areas of the wind farm. The monitoring should help determine whether the additional physical space translates into measurable ecological benefits.The project is part of a wider effort to incorporate nature-inclusive design into offshore infrastructure. Rampion has 116 turbines and a total generating capacity of about 400 megawatts, making the site a useful setting for testing whether conventional engineering requirements can be combined with habitat creation.The RESP project has received support from Innovate UK and involves RWE, ARC marine and other research and engineering partners. Before deployment, the Reef cube design was tested under simulated storm conditions to assess its stability. If monitoring shows that the structures remain effective at controlling scour while supporting diverse marine communities, the approach could provide a model for incorporating habitat features into scour protection at other offshore wind farms.
Article Summary: 75,000 recycled concrete cubes have been installed around the foundation of a wind turbine at the Rampion Offshore Wind Farm, about 13 kilometres off the Sussex coast in the English Channel. The cubes replace conventional rock-based scour protection at one turbine. Developers say the design could provide more than twice the potential habitat volume of traditional rock protection.

Article Title: In 1990, Switzerland crushed an old A13 road and reused its concrete in new pavement; after 20 years, mixes with up to 100% recycled aggregate remained durable
Article Text:
Image AI generated

How the 1990 A13 road project reused old concrete pavement

Recycled concrete aggregate made up 66 to 100% of the test mixes

20-year tests showed strong durability of recycled concrete aggregate

Image AI generated

Recycled concrete aggregate can last 40–50 years

In 1990, the A13 between Oberriet and Haag in the St Gallen Rhine Valley was converted from a motorway to an autobahn, and the 1967 road was completely renewed. Its old concrete pavement was crushed and processed. At the same time, a large-scale experiment put the recycled aggregate into new road concrete, where it made up 66 to 100 per cent by mass. These mixes were compared with a reference concrete made only from natural aggregate. After 20 years of use, all the recycled concretes were still in a good or very good state, according to the report for the Swiss Federal Roads Office.According to the study published in ResearchGate, titled ‘Dauerhaftigkeit von Betonfahrbahnen aus Betongranulat (Durability of concrete pavements of recycled concrete), ’ the A13 between Oberriet and Haag was converted from a motorway to an autobahn in 1990/91. The 1967 road was completely renewed. The former concrete pavement was crushed, processed and used for the cement stabilisation of the underground.At the same time, the report states that a large-scale experiment was started to use the processed concrete aggregate for the new road pavement of the A13. The authors note that for a harsh environment of freezing, de-icing salt and traffic, hardly any experience with recycled concrete was available.They add that concrete from old pavements will become available in increasing amounts in future, and describe recycling these pavements into new ones as an ecologically and economically highly reasonable solution.According to the report, several types of concrete with different amounts of recycled concrete aggregate were manufactured and placed. In these recycled concretes, the recycled aggregate made up between 66 and 100 per cent by mass. Their behaviour was compared with the reference concrete, which contained only aggregate of natural origin.The report distinguishes between two kinds of aggregate preparation. The aggregate of recycled concrete 1a/1b consisted of all-in aggregate rather than separate size fractions. The other recycled concretes used aggregate made from different size fractions: 0/4, 4/8, 8/16 and 16/32. The authors also looked at whether the 0/4 fraction was made from recycled or natural aggregate.According to the report, the recycled concretes and the reference concrete were investigated in detail after 20 years of use. The methods were visual inspection, microscopy, permeability to air, carbonation depth, chloride content, water conductivity, resistance to chloride migration and compressive strength. The goal was to evaluate the durability of recycled concrete in a severe environment of freezing, de-icing salt and traffic.The analyses showed that all types of concrete with recycled aggregate were still "in a good or very good state". Recycled concrete 1a/1b showed slightly worse properties than the other recycled concretes, and the reference concrete performed slightly better than all of them. The report attributes the slight damage to 1a/1b to difficulties during the earlier preparation of the recycled aggregate and during placing and compacting. All the concretes showed a beginning alkali-silica reaction. The authors found no influence on concrete quality from whether the 0/4 fraction was recycled or natural.The report states that all the investigated recycled concrete pavements can continue to be used and are expected to reach an estimated service life of 40 to 50 years, even though the damage will increase. The investigations also showed that recycled concrete made with 100 per cent recycled aggregate can be used for new concrete pavements. The authors stress that this applies only to the aggregate used in this case. If concrete is to be processed into aggregate, it should be tested for possible damage such as alkali-silica reaction and for harmful substances such as de-icing salt.According to the authors, concrete pavements from roads and airfield traffic areas are especially suitable for producing concrete aggregate, because they generally have a high concrete quality and are homogeneous. Building concrete pavements in two layers in future, with recycled concrete aggregate in the lower layer and natural aggregate in the upper layer. The authors say this allows the requirements for noise reduction to be addressed in a more targeted way.
Article Summary: Recycled concrete aggregate made up 66 to 100% of the test mixes. After 20 years of use, all the recycled concretes were still in a good or very good state, according to the report for the Swiss Federal Roads Office. The investigations also showed that recycled concrete made with 100 per cent recycled aggregate can be used for new concrete pavements.

Article Title: A 16-foot Burmese python weighing 147.9 pounds was released after radio-tagging in Florida; US scientists are now testing drones to track invasive snakes across the Everglades
Article Text:
Image: Canva

How United States scientists use drones to monitor invasive Burmese pythons across the Everglades

The 16-foot, 147.9-pound female Burmese python that was radio-tagged

Why Burmese pythons threaten Everglades mammals and why tracking them across difficult terrain is hard (Image: Canva)

How radio tracking equipment and cameras improve python detection efficiency

Why Burmese pythons threaten Everglades mammals and why tracking them across difficult terrain is hard

How drone training for Department of the Interior scientists brought python tracking to the Everglades

Why further testing matters for python control

Deep in the Florida Everglades, a vast and difficult landscape, scientists are trying a new way to find invasive Burmese pythons; they are looking from above. Researchers are testing small drones fitted with radio tracking equipment or cameras to locate snakes more efficiently, follow their movements across difficult terrain, and cut the cost of searching from the ground. One female python released after tagging measured 16 feet and weighed 147.9 pounds. In this article, you will learn how the technology works, why pythons are so hard to track, what the scientists hope to gain, and what important questions remain unanswered.The United States Geological Survey, a federal science agency, is testing a different approach to a long-running wildlife problem. Scientists at its Fort Collins Science Centre are using uncrewed aircraft systems, commonly called drones, to track invasive Burmese pythons and to learn more about how the snakes move across a vast and difficult landscape. The work is described in the center's September 2026 series, which highlights how its projects support sound decision-making. The python project stands out because the agency's own account calls it a novel use of technology that is more commonly applied to monitoring rivers and forests.A photograph published by the USGS captures the technology at work. In the image, agency biologists operate a small uncrewed aircraft system while University of Florida interns release a newly radio-tagged female Burmese python, 16 feet long and weighing 147.9 pounds, back into the Greater Everglades Ecosystem.The scene shows how the pieces fit together: a snake carrying a radio tag, people on the ground handling it safely, and an aircraft overhead testing how well the tag can be followed from the sky.The agency explains that the aircraft can carry either radio tracking equipment or a camera. The platform is being evaluated as a way to improve detection and tracking efficiency, collect better data, and reduce the labour and operating costs of traditional ground-based monitoring for pythons. In plain terms, a drone can cover wet, thick, hard-to-walk areas far faster than a person on foot, and it can pick up a tagged snake's signal or spot the animal from overhead. If it works well, fewer people would need to spend long hours searching difficult ground.The reason for all this effort is the size of the problem. The United States Geological Survey leads federal research to control the Burmese python, which has become firmly established across the Greater Everglades Ecosystem and poses a serious threat to native wildlife. The snake can grow to more than 17 feet long and is believed to be a key factor in the sharp decline of mammal populations in the region. Finding such a well-camouflaged animal in a huge, wet landscape is slow and costly, which explains why scientists are eager to test aerial tools.The idea grew out of a training program. Chris Holmquist-Johnson, a certified instructor in uncrewed aircraft systems for the Department of the Interior, trained a group of Fort Collins Science Centre scientists working in the Florida Everglades about a year before the article was published. Those researchers are now using the technology to track Burmese pythons and are gaining new insight into their movement behaviour. Holmquist-Johnson's main work involves rivers and forests in the western United States, including mapping changes in river channels and surveying thinned forest areas, so the Everglades project shows how skills built in one setting can be carried into another.It is important to read the project for what it is. The agency describes the aircraft as a tool still under evaluation, and the sources do not report measured results, such as how many more snakes are found or how much money is saved. The 16-foot, 147.9-pound snake is a single example from a photograph, not an average, and the agency notes that pythons can grow even longer. As testing continues, the key questions will be how reliably the aircraft locate tagged and untagged snakes, and whether the savings in time and cost hold up across the seasons and the many kinds of habitat in the Everglades.
Article Summary: Scientists at the US Geological Survey are using uncrewed aircraft systems to track invasive Burmese pythons in the Florida Everglades. The platform is being evaluated as a way to improve detection and tracking efficiency, collect better data, and reduce the labour and operating costs of traditional ground-based monitoring. If it works well, fewer people would need to spend long hours searching difficult ground. One female python released after tagging measured 16 feet and weighed 147.9 pounds.

Article Title: Prince William's charitable foundation funded homes on Duchy land in Cornwall; in August, the first phase was handed to a charity, providing accommodation and support for 16 people facing homelessness
Article Text:
As the first residents prepare to move in, the project represents the Duchy of Cornwall’s first housing development specifically designed to address homelessness.

A new beginning in Nansledan

Housing with support at its core

Designed for a lower-carbon future

Poll Vote & Share your view What aspect of the Nansledan project do you find most important? Sustainable building materials Long-term stability for residents 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A wider community taking shape

A new housing project in Cornwall is putting a different face on the fight against homelessness. Rather than treating shelter as a temporary stopgap, the development in Nansledan, Newquay, combines carefully designed homes with practical support, creating a more secure route towards independent living for people who have experienced homelessness. Scroll down to read the details.According to the Nansledan website, on August 4, 2026, St Petrocs received the keys to the first phase of the development from the Duchy of Cornwall. Funded by The Duke of Cornwall’s Charitable Foundation and built on Duchy-owned land, the scheme will provide accommodation for 16 people across two four-bedroom homes and eight one-bedroom apartments.Built by CG Fry & Son, the development was designed around more than simply providing a roof. On-site counselling space will allow St Petrocs to offer residents support alongside their accommodation, helping them establish greater stability as they work towards securing permanent housing, adds the report. The handover marks the completion of the construction phase and the beginning of the homes’ next chapter, with residents set to move into fully equipped properties, the report adds.The project forms part of Homewards, The Royal Foundation’s five-year programme established by The Duke of Cornwall with the ambition of demonstrating that homelessness can be prevented and made rare, brief and unrepeated.The programme brought the Duchy together with homelessness prevention specialists and people with lived experience, helping shape the design and approach to the development. The result is a model that places housing, wellbeing and community connection on the same footing.For St Petrocs, which supports people experiencing homelessness in Cornwall, the homes offer a chance to provide continuity rather than short-term intervention. Residents will have access to personalised support while becoming part of the wider Nansledan community.As per the report, sustainability is another defining feature of the project. The all-electric homes have been constructed with a focus on reducing both embodied carbon and the emissions associated with everyday use. Ultra-low-carbon cement and blockwork, super-insulated hemp-filled wall panels and solar panels form part of the environmental strategy. The approach is intended not only to reduce the development’s impact but also to keep future running costs lower for St Petrocs.The homes have also been furnished through the Homewards Furniture Project, with support from retailers and partners including Howdens, IKEA, DFS, B&Q, Bosch Home Appliances and Gordon Brown’s The Multibank charity. Sofas, tables, chairs, white goods and fitted kitchens mean residents can move into spaces that are ready to live in from day one.Nansledan itself reflects the Duchy’s broader approach to sustainable development. The urban extension to Newquay combines homes with shops, businesses, community facilities, green spaces and walkable neighbourhoods. The supported housing scheme adds another dimension to that vision: ensuring that those at risk of being left on the margins can also find a place within a growing community.As the first residents prepare to move in, the project represents the Duchy of Cornwall’s first housing development specifically designed to address homelessness. Its significance lies not just in the number of homes created, but in the idea behind them: that secure accommodation, meaningful support and a sense of belonging can work together to help people rebuild their lives.Images Courtesy: BBC and Royal Foundation
Article Summary: Nansledan, Newquay, is the Duchy of Cornwall’s first housing development specifically designed to address homelessness. The scheme will provide accommodation for 16 people across two four-bedroom homes and eight one-bedroom apartments. On-site counselling space will allow St Petrocs to offer residents support alongside their accommodation.

Article Title: In 2025, California ran six 100%-recycled-asphalt road sections under a heavy-vehicle simulator; rain-triggered base shear failures and poor moisture control caused sections to fail
Article Text:
Representative AI image showing a heavy-vehicle simulator testing road pavement durability at an outdoor research facility. Image Credits: Google Gemini.

Putting recycled asphalt under extreme traffic

Rain exposed a weakness below the recycled layer

Recycling asphalt can effectively reduce waste, but a California experiment revealed potential complications. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

Moisture control became just as important as recycling

Recycling an old road into a new one can cut waste, reduce the need for fresh aggregates and extend the life of asphalt materials. But a large-scale California experiment in 2025 produced a more complicated result. When pavement made with 100% reclaimed asphalt pavement was subjected to simulated heavy traffic, some sections failed sooner than expected, highlighting the importance of water, construction quality and the strength of the layers underneath.According to the University of California Pavement Research Centre , a Heavy Vehicle Simulator (HVS) was used to repeatedly load pavement sections with heavy wheels during the experiment. Six tests were carried out on a specially constructed track to examine cold recycled pavement made with 100% recycled asphalt pavement. The results did not show that the recycled asphalt itself caused the failures. Instead, investigators linked the most serious problems to localised shear failures in the aggregate base after heavy rainfall and to incorrect water contents in part of one recycled layer.The test track was designed to reproduce the stresses roads experience from repeated heavy vehicles.The pavement structure included a 225 mm aggregate subbase, a 180 mm aggregate base, a 120 mm cold recycled layer and a 60 mm rubberised hot-mix asphalt surface. The recycled layer used reclaimed asphalt pavement as its material and was produced using different recycling agents, including emulsified and foamed asphalt.The researchers tested the sections at two pavement temperatures, about 30°C and 50°C, and under two moisture conditions. Some sections were tested as compacted, while others were exposed to a constant flow of water. Traffic loading continued until a section reached either 12.5 mm of terminal rutting or a specified level of cracking. The results varied widely. The number of equivalent single-axle loads needed to reach terminal rutting ranged from about 200,000 to more than 15 million. The section that failed at the lowest traffic level was tested at high temperature and already had construction problems with foaming water and mixing moisture.The investigation provided one of the clearest lessons from the experiment. Heavy rainfall caused water to enter the pavement structure, and localised shear failures developed in the aggregate base. Once that underlying layer weakened, repeated heavy loading could cause substantial deformation even if the recycled asphalt layer itself was not the source of the problem.This matters because cold recycled asphalt mixtures can have relatively high void content and need protection from water. Earlier field and laboratory work has shown that pavement design, climate and the thickness of adjacent layers can strongly influence the performance of cold recycled pavements. A study published in the Journal of Cleaner Production has also found that climate and pavement structure are important factors in the performance of cold central-plant and cold in-place recycled pavements, while these recycling approaches have offered substantial reductions in energy use and greenhouse-gas emissions.Another major problem emerged during production of the cold central-plant recycled material. Investigators found that the foaming-water and mixing-moisture contents used in part of one test lane were incorrect. Too much or too little water can affect how recycled material is mixed, compacted and performs under traffic.According to the California report , foamed-asphalt recycling depends on carefully controlled water content, as water is used to create the foam that helps distribute the asphalt binder through reclaimed pavement. The study found that the optimum foaming-water and mixing-moisture levels established during mix design had to be reproduced during construction. Departures from those levels in either direction could affect the performance of the recycled layer.The California experiment ultimately delivered a more useful message than a simple success-or-failure story. According to the researchers, properly designed and constructed cold recycled layers can perform well. But pavements with marginal aggregate bases that are vulnerable to shear failure when wet need extra attention, especially where heavy axle loads and extreme weather are expected.
Article Summary: Recycling asphalt can effectively reduce waste, but a California experiment revealed potential complications. Heavy rainfall caused water to enter the pavement structure, and localised shear failures developed in the aggregate base. Once that underlying layer weakened, repeated heavy loading could cause substantial deformation even if the recycled asphalt layer itself was not the source of the problem.

Article Title: A 21-year-old Mexican environmental innovator is developing microbial fuel cells that use discarded materials to generate electricity and improve polluted water; her project aims to produce 50 working
Article Text:
Maritza Sanchez Photo credit: https://www.broweryouthawards.org/winner/maritza-sanchez/

A problem close to home

How microbial fuel cells work

Building and testing prototypes

Recognition and a next phase

A local idea with a measurable goal

Growing up in Cuautlancingo, a town in Mexico’s Puebla state, Maritza Sanchez saw pollution close to home. Now 21, she is developing microbial fuel cells that use materials recovered from local waste to generate electricity and help improve polluted water. Her project, Aquayac Energy, is focused on the Atoyac River, one of the waterways affected by serious contamination. The goal is ambitious but specific: refine her prototypes and produce 50 functional fuel cells by 2027. Earth Island Institute announced Sanchez as one of the 2026 Brower Youth Award winners, recognising her work alongside five other young environmental leaders. The award highlights not a finished technology, but a young innovator testing whether a small-scale, locally designed system can address two urgent needs at once: cleaner water and access to energy.Sanchez’s interest in pollution grew from what she observed around her. Earth Island Institute’s announcement says Cuautlancingo is surrounded by pollution, and that this experience helped shape her idea as a high school student. She began exploring whether discarded materials could be repurposed into a system that might both produce electricity and improve water quality.The project centres on the Atoyac River, which is heavily contaminated.Water pollution can affect communities in many ways, from the health of the river ecosystem to the quality of water people encounter in their daily lives. Sanchez’s idea is to test whether microbial fuel cells could offer a local tool for treating some wastewater while generating useful energy.Her project is called Aquayac Energy. The name reflects its connection to the Atoyac and the effort to turn an environmental challenge into a practical experiment. Rather than approaching pollution only as a problem to document, Sanchez is building and testing a technology that could make use of materials already available in the community, as per the report.Microbial fuel cells use microorganisms to break down organic matter. As microbes consume that material, they release electrons, which can be captured by electrodes and used to generate a small electrical current. In Sanchez’s concept, the system uses discarded local materials and wastewater as part of the process. The technology is being researched in different settings, but Sanchez’s work is at the prototype stage. She designs and constructs the cells, tests their performance and measures how much energy they produce. She also examines water quality after treatment, assessing whether the process changes the condition of the water, it further shared.Those measurements matter because producing electricity alone would not make a system useful if it did not also treat water effectively. Similarly, a treatment process would need to be assessed for safety, consistency and suitability before anyone could rely on it. Sanchez’s work therefore involves testing more than one outcome, with the design still being refined.The technology is not a substitute for large-scale wastewater infrastructure or comprehensive river clean-up. Instead, it is an early-stage effort to see whether a compact, locally built system can contribute to solutions in places facing pollution and limited access to energy.Through Aquayac Energy, Sanchez has been designing, constructing and testing microbial fuel cell prototypes. The work includes checking the quality of water after treatment and measuring the amount of electricity the cells generate. These tests help her understand what is working, where the design needs improvement and whether the results can be repeated.The challenge is partly technical and partly practical. A successful prototype must function reliably, use materials that can be sourced and maintained, and produce results that can be measured. If the system is eventually used in communities, it would also need to be safe and suited to local conditions.That is why Sanchez’s 2027 target is framed around working units. She expects to scale the project over the coming year and produce 50 functional fuel cells. The goal provides a concrete measure of progress, moving beyond a concept towards a larger group of prototypes that can be evaluated.The award announcement does not claim that the cells are already supplying electricity to households or that they have solved pollution in the Atoyac. Instead, it describes an ongoing effort to refine the design and test its environmental and energy outcomes.Earth Island Institute selected Sanchez as one of six 2026 Brower Youth Award recipients. The annual award recognises young leaders whose work is contributing to environmental change in North America and beyond. The institute said the projects recognised this year ranged from habitat restoration and pollinator protection to school climate action and technologies for wastewater.The award also offers more than public recognition. Earth Island Institute says recipients receive leadership training, networking opportunities and a platform to amplify their work. For a project still developing its prototypes, those connections may help Sanchez share results, find collaborators and build support for the next stage.Sanchez’s work stands out because it brings together environmental concerns that are often handled separately. Waste, water quality and energy access each demand their own solutions, but her project asks whether one process might help with more than one of them. Whether microbial fuel cells can make a lasting contribution will depend on what further testing shows.The most immediate milestone is the planned production of 50 functional fuel cells by 2027. Reaching that target would allow Sanchez to work with more units, gather additional data and better understand how the technology performs. It would not, by itself, establish that the system is ready for widespread use, but it could take the project from early experimentation to a more substantial stage of evaluation.Sanchez’s approach begins with the conditions around her. She is responding to pollution in her community by designing a technology that draws on local discarded materials and targets wastewater. The work combines invention with careful measurement, checking both energy generation and water quality rather than relying on promises.For now, Aquayac Energy remains a project in development. Its significance lies in the questions it is testing and the commitment to build, measure and refine the technology. At 21, Sanchez is turning a concern rooted in her home region into an engineering challenge with a clear next step: 50 working units, and better evidence about what they can do.
Article Summary: Maritza Sanchez is developing microbial fuel cells that use materials recovered from local waste to generate electricity and help improve polluted water. Her project, Aquayac Energy, is focused on the Atoyac River, one of the waterways affected by serious contamination. The goal is ambitious but specific: refine her prototypes and produce 50 functional fuel cells by 2027. Earth Island Institute announced Sanchez as a 2026 Brower Youth Award winner.

Article Title: Florida put radioactive fertiliser waste beneath a private road; 4 test sections are being monitored for safety

How will the Florida road project be monitored for safety

PC: AI Generated

Why is the material considered a radiation and health concern

How are stacks designed to limit exposure

Other uses of phosphogypsum under EPA rules

A waste material from fertiliser production is being tested for a new use in road construction in Florida. The material, known as phosphogypsum, is produced when phosphate ore is processed to make phosphoric acid. It contains radium, which can decay into radioactive radon gas, so its use is regulated by the US Environmental Protection Agency. The EPA generally requires phosphogypsum to be managed in engineered stacks that limit public exposure. However, some other uses can be approved when they provide at least as much protection.According to the US Environmental Protection Agency, one such project in New Wales, Florida, uses phosphogypsum in the road base beneath asphalt on private property. The agency determined that the project was as protective of human health as stacking the material.The EPA approved a phosphogypsum road construction project for Mosaic Fertilizer, LLC on December 23, 2024. The project is located on private property in New Wales, Florida. Phosphogypsum will be incorporated into the road base and covered with asphalt. The test road has four sections containing phosphogypsum in the road base, separated by four control sections without phosphogypsum.One upgradient monitoring well and two downgradient wells will be placed in each section. The property has controlled access, so members of the public are not expected to come into contact with the phosphogypsum in the test road. The EPA approved the request after determining that the proposed use was as protective of human health as placement of phosphogypsum in a stack.Phosphogypsum is produced when phosphate ore is processed to make phosphoric acid, which is later used in fertilizer. The phosphate ore and the resulting phosphogypsum contain radium. Radium decays to form radon gas, which is radioactive and can cause cancer.The EPA says radon in outside air can enter structures and reach levels that pose a health hazard over time. Higher exposure to radon over prolonged periods can increase the risk of developing lung cancer. Phosphogypsum stacks also contain low-pH process water and heavy metals. Because radionuclides in phosphogypsum are a source of radon gas and direct gamma radiation, the EPA regulates phosphogypsum as a source category of radionuclides under the Clean Air Act.EPA regulations generally require phosphogypsum to be managed in engineered stacks to limit public exposure from radon emissions. Owners and operators of inactive stacks must measure and report radon emissions and keep those emissions within regulatory limits. When phosphogypsum is placed on a stack, it is added as a liquid slurry.As the stack dewaters, the liquid effluent is captured, treated, tested, and discharged under the Clean Water Act. Newer stacks contain a liner to help prevent effluent from being released directly into soil and groundwater, while older stacks may not. When inactive, an engineered cover is typically placed over the phosphogypsum to prevent further water infiltration.EPA regulations allow phosphogypsum to be removed from stacks for outdoor agricultural purposes and indoor research and development under certain conditions and restrictions. Any other use requires prior EPA approval formally. The agency evaluates each proposed use case by case, considering how the phosphogypsum would be used, the amount involved, and possible health risks to workers and the public, including risks from handling and transportation. EPA can approve a proposed use only when it is at least as protective of public health as placing phosphogypsum in a stack.
Article Summary: Phosphogypsum is produced when phosphate ore is processed to make phosphoric acid. It contains radium, which can decay into radioactive radon gas. The material is regulated by the US Environmental Protection Agency. Project in New Wales, Florida, uses the material in the road base beneath asphalt on private property.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption.
